title: Explaining the turban
hookLine: Sikhs around the world invite neighbors to learn about the turban

lines: A TABLE ON A COLLEGE LAWN.
cards: Why do you wear that every single day? On a college lawn, a student finally asks. There's a folding table, bright lengths of cloth at one end, a mirror at the other, and a hand-lettered sign: ask us anything.

A Sikh volunteer smiles and starts winding a long cloth around the student's head, explaining each fold as they go. Minutes later the student is looking in the mirror, a little surprised, still waiting for the answer.
Sikhs hold days like this on campuses and in town squares around the world. Today: the answer they give.

teach.b: First, the name. In Punjabi the turban is the dastar, and in everyday speech a pagg.
For a Sikh who wears one, it covers the kesh, the uncut hair: the Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, asks Sikhs to keep their hair uncut, and the turban keeps it covered. Second, the text.

In a hymn of Guru Arjan, at Ang 1084 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru describes, in the words of his Muslim neighbors, what makes a true Muslim, and among its pictures is a form kept whole, with the dastar on the head.

The lines around it speak of a heart as soft as wax, and of truth. Sikhs often point to that line when they explain the turban, and notice where it sits: beside inner things, not apart from them. Third, the meaning.
Some Sikhs call it a crown, a gift from the Guru. Some speak of a promise worn in public, which makes it harder to break quietly.

teach.h: A CROWN, A PROMISE, EASY TO FIND.
teach.b: Tradition says the Gurus wanted a Sikh to be easy to find in a crowd, so that anyone in trouble would know whom to ask for help. Some Sikh women wear a turban too; others cover their hair with a long scarf, a chunni.
Fourth, the invitation. Sikhs have been taken for people they are not, and sometimes harassed for it.

teach.h: AN OPEN TABLE, NOT A COMPLAINT.
teach.b: So some gurdwaras and student groups answer with an open table instead of a complaint.
Their bet is simple: a neighbor who has asked one real question, and heard one real answer, looks at a turban differently afterward.

how: Sikhs who wear the turban tie it fresh, usually each morning, over uncut hair; some gurdwaras and Sikh student groups hold turban days where neighbors can ask questions and try one on.

games.why: at turban days, Sikhs invite exactly this: one real question, then one real answer. ask, then learn.

practice: Choose the one fact from today you didn't know before, the word dastar, the hymn at Ang 1084, or why a Sikh might want to be easy to find in a crowd, and hold it gently, the way the volunteer held the cloth.
Say it to yourself on the breath in and let it settle on the breath out; if you pray, you can say Waheguru instead.

wordCard.voice: Dastar. The Punjabi word for the turban that covers uncut hair, named in a hymn of Guru Arjan. Today's word.
